front: What is a σ-algebra on a set Ω?
back: A collection F of subsets of Ω with three properties: Ω is in F (S1); the complement of each member of F is in F (S2); and the union of each countable sequence of members of F is in F (S3). Its members are the events (Definition 1.1).

front: What is an event?
back: A member of the σ-algebra F on Ω (Definition 1.1). Probability is defined only on events.

front: What is a partition of Ω?
back: A family B_1, …, B_k of non-empty, pairwise disjoint sets whose union is Ω. Its members are its blocks (Section 2).

front: What does Proposition 1.3 give for a σ-algebra F on Ω?
back: Assumptions: F is a σ-algebra on Ω, and A, B, A_1, A_2, … are members of F. Statement: (a) the empty set is in F; (b) A ∪ B and A ∩ B are in F; (c) the intersection of a countable sequence of members of F is in F.

front: What is the σ-algebra generated by a partition with k blocks, and how many events does it have?
back: Assumptions: Ω is a set, and B_1, …, B_k (k ≥ 1) is a partition of Ω. It is the family of all unions U_J of blocks, with U_∅ = ∅. Proposition 2.1: it is a σ-algebra on Ω with exactly 2^k members, and it is the smallest σ-algebra that contains the blocks.

front: Is the family of finite and cofinite subsets of N = {1, 2, 3, …} a σ-algebra, although it is closed under finite unions?
back: No. It is closed under complements and finite unions but not under countable unions. The singletons {2n} are members, and their union, the even positive integers, is neither finite nor cofinite (Example 3.1).

front: What counts does Lab 1 print for the three partitions?
back: 4 members for blocks {0,1} and {2,3} on the four-point set; 16 for four singleton blocks; 8 for blocks {0,1}, {2,3}, {4,5} on the six-point set.
basis: Lab 1, basis: exhaustive enumeration of finite families

front: Is any collection of subsets that contains Ω a σ-algebra?
back: No. Definition 1.1 also requires (S2) and (S3). The collection {empty set, {1}, Ω} on {1, 2, 3} contains Ω and fails (S2), because the complement {2, 3} of {1} is missing (Example 1.2).

front: Is every subset of Ω an event, whatever Ω and the collection are?
back: No. The events are the members of the chosen σ-algebra. On the four-point set, the σ-algebra generated by the blocks {0,1} and {2,3} has 4 members, not the 16 subsets (Proposition 2.1(b)).

front: What is a measure on (Ω, F)?
back: A function μ from F to [0, ∞] with (M1) μ(empty set) = 0 and (M2) countable additivity: for a countable sequence of pairwise disjoint events, μ of their union is the sum of the μ values (Definition 1.1).

front: What is a probability space?
back: A triple (Ω, F, P) where F is a σ-algebra on Ω and P is a measure on (Ω, F) with P(Ω) = 1 (Definition 1.2).

front: What do finite additivity and monotonicity say for a measure μ?
back: Assumptions: (Ω, F) is a σ-algebra with a measure μ, and A, B, A_1, A_2, … are events. (a) For pairwise disjoint A_1, …, A_m, μ of their union is the sum of the μ(A_i). (b) If A ⊆ B, then μ(A) ≤ μ(B) (Proposition 1.3).

front: For a probability space and an event A, what are P(A^c) and the range of P(A)?
back: Assumptions: (Ω, F, P) is a probability space and A is an event. Then P(A^c) = 1 − P(A), and 0 ≤ P(A) ≤ 1 (Proposition 1.5).

front: On a finite Ω with all subsets as events, which functions define probability measures?
back: Assumptions: Ω = {ω_1, …, ω_n} is finite and F is the collection of all subsets. (a) Any p with p(ω) ≥ 0 and total sum 1 defines P(A) = sum of p over A, which is a probability measure. (b) Every probability measure is of this form, with p(ω) = P({ω}) (Proposition 2.1).

front: Is P(A ∪ B) always P(A) + P(B) for events A and B?
back: Assumptions: (Ω, F, P) is a probability space, and A, B are events. Then P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B) (Proposition 3.1), so the sum holds only when A and B are disjoint, or when their overlap has probability zero. For the fair die, P({1,2}) + P({2,3}) = 2/3, but P({1,2,3}) = 1/2.

front: What does Lab 2 print for six weights of 3/20?
back: The 3/20 weights are non-negative and additive, and they sum to 9/10, so total mass one fails.
basis: Lab 2, basis: exhaustive enumeration of the six-point space

front: Is a function from events to [0, 1] that gives Ω the value one a probability measure?
back: No. ν(A) = (|A|/6)² on the six-point set gives Ω the value one and takes values in [0, 1], but it is not additive: ν({1,2}) = 4/36, while ν({1}) + ν({2}) = 2/36 (Example 2.3).

front: Is an event with probability zero impossible?
back: No. Under the point-mass measure with all weight on face 1, the non-empty event {2} has probability zero (Example 2.2).

front: When is a function f from Ω to [0, ∞] measurable?
back: When, for every real t, the set {f > t} is an event. Then {f ≥ t} is an event too, as a countable intersection (Section 1).

front: What is a simple function?
back: A measurable function s from Ω to [0, ∞) that takes finitely many values a_1, …, a_m, on the events A_i = {s = a_i}, which partition Ω. Its canonical representation is s = sum of a_i times the indicator of A_i (Definition 1.1).

front: What is the integral of a simple function s against μ?
back: The sum of a_i μ(A_i) over the canonical representation, with the convention 0 · ∞ = 0 (Definition 2.1).

front: Is the integral of simple functions monotone?
back: Assumptions: (Ω, F, μ) is a measure space, and s and t are simple with s ≤ t on Ω. Then the integral of s is at most the integral of t (Proposition 2.2).

front: What is the Lebesgue integral of a measurable f from Ω to [0, ∞]?
back: The supremum of the integrals of simple functions s with 0 ≤ s ≤ f. It is an element of [0, ∞] (Definition 3.1).

front: Does the Lebesgue integral agree with the simple-function integral, and is it monotone?
back: Assumptions: (Ω, F, μ) is a measure space; f and g are measurable from Ω to [0, ∞]; s is simple. (a) For simple s, the supremum of Definition 3.1 equals the integral of Definition 2.1. (b) If f ≤ g, then the integral of f is at most that of g (Proposition 3.2).

front: Does changing a simple function's value at a point of measure zero change its integral?
back: Assumptions: {x_0} is an event with μ({x_0}) = 0; s is simple; s' equals s except at x_0, where s'(x_0) = c for some c in [0, ∞). Then s' is simple and has the same integral as s (Proposition 3.3).

front: What is Assumption L, the length measure on [0, 1]?
back: The events of [0, 1] form a σ-algebra containing every interval, and a measure λ on it satisfies λ([a, b]) = b − a for 0 ≤ a ≤ b ≤ 1. The lesson assumes this and does not prove it.

front: How do the dyadic simple functions s_n(x) = 2^(−n) floor(2^n x²) bracket the integral of x² on [0, 1]?
back: Assumptions: Assumption L holds, λ is the length measure, and n ≥ 1. Then s_n is simple, and 0 ≤ s_n(x) ≤ x² ≤ s_n(x) + 2^(−n) on [0, 1]. With I_n the sum over k from 0 to 2^n − 1 of (k/2^n)(sqrt((k+1)/2^n) − sqrt(k/2^n)), I_n ≤ integral of x² ≤ I_n + 2^(−n) (Proposition 4.1).

front: What does Lab 3 print for the step function?
back: Part A: the step function with values 0, 1 and 3 on pieces of length 1/2, 1/4 and 1/4 has integral 1, and adding a one-point piece of value 5 at the point 1/2 (length 0) leaves the integral at 1.

front: Is x² a simple function because it is a polynomial?
back: No. A simple function takes finitely many values, and x² takes every value in [0, 1]. Its integral is defined through the supremum of Definition 3.1, and, under Assumption L, Proposition 4.1 brackets that integral from below and above.

front: Does a dyadic approximation at a finite level give the integral of x² exactly?
back: No. At n = 1, I_1 ≈ 0.1464, while the calculus value 1/3 ≈ 0.3333 of the integral of x² is not proved on the page to equal the Lebesgue integral. The gap 1/3 − I_1 ≈ 0.1869 lies inside the bound 2^(−1) = 0.5 but is far from zero.
basis: Lab 3, basis: floating-point numerical check in Part B

front: What does it mean for functions f_n from Ω to [0, ∞] to be non-decreasing and to converge pointwise?
back: Non-decreasing means f_n ≤ f_{n+1} for each n. Pointwise convergence means f_n(ω) → f(ω) for each ω, as a limit in [0, ∞]. For a non-decreasing sequence the limit exists and equals the supremum of the f_n(ω) (Definition 1.1).

front: What does the monotone convergence theorem state?
back: Assumptions: (Ω, F, μ) is a measure space; each f_n is measurable from Ω to [0, ∞]; the sequence is non-decreasing; and f = lim f_n pointwise. Statement: f is measurable, and the integral of f_n converges to the integral of f in [0, ∞] (Theorem 2.1).

front: What does the dominated convergence theorem state, and is it proved in the lesson?
back: It is stated and not proved on the page. Assumptions: f_n and f are real measurable functions; f_n → f at every point; and some measurable g ≥ 0 has finite integral with |f_n| ≤ g for every n. Conclusion: f is integrable and the integrals of f_n converge to the integral of f (Theorem 3.1).

front: Must a dominating function be bounded?
back: No. On (0, 1] with f_n(x) = min(n, x^(−1/2)), the function g = x^(−1/2) dominates every f_n and is unbounded. Its calculus integral is 2, and the integral of f_n is 2 − 1/n, which tends to 2. The example assumes that the calculus value is the Lebesgue integral (Example 3.2).
basis: Lesson 4, Example 3.2 (calculus antiderivative; identity with the Lebesgue integral assumed)

front: Can an integrable function dominate n·1{(0, 1/n]} on (0, 1]?
back: No. Assumptions: λ is the length measure on [0, 1]; f_n = n·1{(0, 1/n]}; and g is measurable with g ≥ f_n on (0, 1] for every n. Then the integral of g is infinite, so no integrable bound exists (Proposition 4.1).

front: For f_n = n·1{(0, 1/n]} on [0, 1], do the integrals of f_n converge to the integral of their pointwise limit?
back: No. Assuming Assumption L (λ is the length measure on [0, 1]), each integral is 1 while the pointwise limit is 0 at every point, so the limit of the integrals is 1 and the integral of the limit is 0 (Proposition 4.2).

front: Does Lab 4 confirm that the integral of n·1{(0, 1/n]} is 1 for each n from 1 to 20?
back: Yes. The integrals equal 1 for n from 1 to 20 (Lab 4, Part A). The general case, under Assumption L, is Proposition 4.2(a).
basis: Lab 4, basis: exact fraction computation over the listed values

front: Does monotone convergence apply to every convergent sequence of functions?
back: No. Theorem 2.1 needs a non-decreasing sequence. For f_n = n·1{(0, 1/n]}, f_1 ≤ f_2 fails (Example 2.2).

front: What is Fubini's theorem as this lesson uses the term?
back: The statement that, for a function f on a product of two measure spaces, the integral against the product measure equals each of the two iterated integrals, in either order, provided an integrability hypothesis holds. Theorem 1.2 proves the finite case, and Assumption F gives the general form (Definition 1.1).

front: Do the two iterated sums and the double sum agree for a function on a finite product?
back: Assumptions: X and Y are finite; μ1 and μ2 are non-negative weights, with μ(x,y) = μ1(x) μ2(y); f is real on X × Y. Then I_1 = sum of f μ = I_2 (Theorem 1.2). The proof uses only the distributive law, the commutativity and associativity of multiplication, and the commutativity and associativity of finite sums.

front: What is the general Fubini statement (Assumption F)?
back: Assumptions: the two spaces are σ-finite; f is measurable for the product σ-algebra; and the integral of |f| is finite. Conclusion: both iterated integrals of f exist and equal the integral of f. It is stated, not proved, and not graded.

front: What does Assumption T (Tonelli) say for nonnegative functions?
back: For f ≥ 0 measurable for the product σ-algebra, under the σ-finiteness of Assumption F, the two iterated integrals are equal as values in [0, ∞], with no integrability hypothesis. It is stated, not proved, and not used in any proof on the page.

front: For f(x,y) = (x² − y²)/(x² + y²)² on [0, 1]², what are the two iterated integrals?
back: Assumptions: f is as defined, with the origin excluded, and the fundamental theorem of calculus is used. For x > 0 the integral over y is 1/(1 + x²); for y > 0 the integral over x is −1/(1 + y²). So the y-integral taken first and then x gives π/4, and the x-integral taken first and then y gives −π/4 (Proposition 3.1).

front: Is f from Proposition 3.1 integrable on the unit square?
back: No. Assumptions: f is as defined. The blocks Q_k = (a_k, 2a_k] × [0, a_k], with a_k = 2^(−(k+1)), lie in the square, and f ≥ 0 on each block. Assumption C (for a function continuous on a closed rectangle, the integral equals either iterated integral) and the additivity and monotonicity of the integral are used without proof. The integrals of f⁺ and f⁻ over the square are both infinite, so the integral of |f| is infinite (Proposition 3.2).

front: If both iterated integrals of a function exist, must they be equal?
back: No. For the function of Proposition 3.1, both iterated integrals exist and are finite, with values +π/4 and −π/4, so they differ.

front: Does Fubini's theorem need only the existence of each iterated integral?
back: No. Assumption F requires that the integral of |f| is finite. For the function of Proposition 3.1 that integral is infinite (Proposition 3.2), so the theorem gives no equality.

front: Does agreement of quadrature with ±π/4 justify interchanging the integrals?
back: No. Agreement with each closed form, to about 10^(−7), tests two one-dimensional integrals. It does not test that the integral of |f| is finite, and Proposition 3.2 shows that it is not.

front: What is the integral of f over each block Q_k, and what does it imply?
back: Each block Q_k has the same integral, arctan 2 − π/4 ≈ 0.3217505544. Since the blocks are disjoint and the positive parts add, the integral of f⁺ is infinite (Proposition 3.2).

front: When is a measure ν absolutely continuous with respect to μ (ν ≪ μ)?
back: When μ(A) = 0 implies ν(A) = 0 for every event A. In plain words, ν gives no weight to any event that μ regards as having no weight (Definition 1.1).

front: On a finite set, when does ν ≪ μ hold?
back: Assumptions: Ω is finite, and μ and ν are measures given by non-negative weights. ν ≪ μ holds if and only if ν(ω) = 0 at each point ω with μ(ω) = 0 (Lemma 1.2).

front: What is a density of ν with respect to μ?
back: A function f ≥ 0 on Ω with ν(A) equal to the integral of f over A against μ, which on a finite set is the sum of f(ω) μ(ω) over A, for every event A (Definition 2.1).

front: What is the general Radon-Nikodym statement (Assumption RN)?
back: Assumptions: μ and ν are σ-finite, and ν ≪ μ. Conclusion: a measurable density f ≥ 0 exists, unique up to a μ-null set. It is stated, not proved, and not graded.

front: On a finite set, when does a density exist, and what is it?
back: Assumptions: Ω is finite; μ and ν are measures given by non-negative weights; ν ≪ μ. Then f(ω) = ν(ω)/μ(ω) where μ(ω) > 0, and f(ω) = 0 where μ(ω) = 0, is a density of ν with respect to μ (Theorem 2.2(a)).

front: On a finite set with ν ≪ μ and density f, what is the integral of a real function g against ν?
back: Assumptions: Ω is finite; μ and ν are non-negative weights with ν ≪ μ; f is a density; g is any real function. Then the sum of g ν equals the sum of g f μ (Proposition 2.2).

front: When can no density exist?
back: Assumptions: Ω is finite; μ and ν are given by non-negative weights; and some ω_0 has μ(ω_0) = 0 < ν(ω_0). Then no function g ≥ 0 is a density of ν with respect to μ, because the event {ω_0} has μ-measure zero while ν of it is positive (Proposition 2.3).

front: Is a density always a probability, with values between 0 and 1?
back: No. A density is a ratio ν(ω)/μ(ω) where μ is positive, and it can exceed 1. On a four-point space with μ positive everywhere, Lab 1 Part A gives the values 2, 1/2, 2 and 1/3 (Remark 2.4).
basis: Lab 1, basis: exact fraction computation in Part A

front: Are any two measures on a finite set related by a density?
back: No. On a finite set with μ and ν given by non-negative weights, μ = 0 at point 5 and ν(5) = 1/8, so no density exists (Proposition 2.3).

front: Is the density unique at every point?
back: No. Theorem 2.2(b) fixes the density only where μ(ω) > 0. Where μ(ω) = 0, the density can take any non-negative value, and no integral changes.

front: Which random variables are measurable for the σ-algebra generated by a partition?
back: Assumptions: Ω is finite; G is generated by a partition of Ω into cells; Z is real on Ω. Statement: Z is G-measurable if and only if Z is constant on each cell. Then Z is the sum of c_j times the indicator of B_j, where c_j is the value of Z on B_j (Proposition 1.1).

front: What is the conditional expectation of X given G in L2?
back: The G-measurable random variable Y that minimizes E[(X − Y)²] over all G-measurable Y. It is the orthogonal projection of X onto the G-measurable functions, meaning that X − Y has E[(X − Y)Z] = 0 for every G-measurable Z (Definition 2.1).

front: On a finite space with a partition, what is E[X | G] and why is it the best estimate?
back: Assumptions: Ω is finite with weights p(ω) > 0 summing to 1; G is generated by a partition B_1, …, B_m with P(B_j) > 0; X is a random variable. The cell average Y = E[X 1_{B_j}]/P(B_j) on each B_j is the unique minimizer of E[(X − Y')²] over G-measurable Y', and it is the only G-measurable Y with E[(X − Y)Z] = 0 for every G-measurable Z (Theorem 2.2).

front: For nested partitions, what is E[E[X | G] | H]?
back: Assumptions: Ω is finite with positive weights; G is generated by a partition {B_j}; H by a coarser partition {C_i} whose cells are unions of the B_j; X is a random variable. Then E[E[X | G] | H] = E[X | H]. With H trivial, E[E[X | G]] = E[X] (Proposition 2.4).

front: What is conditional expectation on a general space (Assumption CE)?
back: For integrable X and a sub-σ-algebra G, a G-measurable Y with E[X 1_A] = E[Y 1_A] for every A in G, unique up to a set of probability zero. It is stated, not proved, and not graded.

front: Is E[X | G] a single number?
back: No. It is a G-measurable random variable, constant on each cell (Definition 2.1; Proposition 1.1).

front: What are the cell averages in the Lab 1 example?
back: 1 on the cell {0, 1, 2}, 6/5 on {3, 4} and 6/7 on {5, 6, 7} (Lab 1 Part A).
basis: Lab 1, basis: exact cell averages in Part A

front: Is E[X | G] the value of X at the outcome that occurred?
back: No. It is the average of X over the cell that contains the outcome. On the cell {0, 1, 2}, X takes the values 2, −1 and 4, with probabilities 1/16, 2/16 and 1/16 on outcomes 0, 1 and 2. The conditional expectation there is the probability-weighted average (2·1 − 1·2 + 4·1)/4 = 1, which Part A of Lab 1 prints as 1.
basis: Lab 1, Part A: exact fraction computation with the stated weights

front: Does conditioning on the finer information and then on the coarser give the finer answer?
back: No. For nested partitions on a finite space with positive weights, E[E[X | G] | H] = E[X | H], the coarser answer (Proposition 2.4). Part D of Lab 1 checks this on the two cells of H.

front: What is a filtration on Ω?
back: A family F_0 ⊆ F_1 ⊆ … ⊆ F_N of sub-σ-algebras of the power set of Ω, each generated by a partition, so that information is never lost as time passes (Definition 1.1).

front: What is the natural filtration of a process?
back: The natural filtration has F_k generated by the record (X_0, …, X_k) (Definition 1.2).

front: What are the properties of the natural filtration of the ±1 walk?
back: Assumptions: the walk has paths of length N with weights from a fixed p in (0, 1), and F_k is generated by the prefix of length k. (a) F_0 is {empty set, Ω}, and F_N contains every subset. (b) F_k ⊆ F_(k+1). (c) S_k is F_k-measurable, so the walk is adapted (Proposition 2.1).

front: What is a martingale on a filtration (F_k)?
back: An adapted process (M_k) with E[M_(k+1) | F_k] = M_k for each k from 0 to N−1, where the conditional expectation is the L2 conditional expectation of L07 (Definition 2.2).

front: How is the martingale property tested on cells?
back: Assumptions: (M_k) is adapted to the natural filtration of the walk, and each cell at time k has positive probability. (M_k) is a martingale if and only if, for each level-k cell B, the average E[M_(k+1) 1_B]/P(B) equals the value of M_k on B (Proposition 2.2).

front: What is the increment of the ±1 walk on a cell, and when is the walk a martingale?
back: Assumptions: the walk has steps with probability p in (0, 1) and its natural filtration. For each k < N and each level-k cell B with prefix h, the average of S_(k+1) over B is S_k(h) + (2p − 1). So the walk is a martingale if and only if p = 1/2 (Proposition 2.3).

front: On the natural filtration of the walk, is the expectation of a martingale constant in time?
back: Yes. E[M_k] = E[M_0] for each k. Problem P3 gives the argument, which uses the trivial-partition case of Proposition 2.4 of L07.

front: Does the fair walk pass the cell test on the ten-step tree?
back: Yes. The fair walk passes all 1023 cells at levels 0 to 9 (Lab 1 Part B).
basis: Lab 1, Part B (exact enumeration of the ten-step tree)

front: Is a process with zero expected increments a martingale?
back: No. Let M_0 = 0, M_1 = X_1 with X_1 fair, and M_2 = 2X_1. Then E[M_2 − M_1] = E[X_1] = 0, but E[M_2 | F_1] = 2X_1 ≠ X_1 = M_1.

front: Does the natural filtration reveal the whole path from time 0?
back: No. At time k it reveals the first k steps. At time 0 it is the trivial family {empty set, Ω} (Proposition 2.1(a)).

front: Is M_k = S_k − k(2p − 1) a martingale only when p = 1/2?
back: No. The compensated walk is a martingale for every p in (0, 1). On each cell its average next value is S_k(h) + (2p − 1) − (k + 1)(2p − 1) = M_k(h). Problem P2 gives the argument.

front: What is a stopping time for a filtration (F_k)?
back: A random time τ with values in {0, 1, 2, …} ∪ {∞} such that {τ ≤ k} is in F_k for every whole number k ≥ 0 (Definition 9.1).

front: Is the first hitting time of a set B by an adapted integer process a stopping time?
back: Assumptions: (Ω, F, P) is a probability space; (F_k) is a filtration; X is an integer-valued process adapted to (F_k), so that {X_k = b} is in F_k for each k and each integer b; B is a set of integers; τ_B = inf{k ≥ 0 : X_k in B}, with inf of the empty set equal to ∞. Then τ_B is a stopping time (Proposition 9.5).

front: Are the minimum, maximum and shift of stopping times stopping times?
back: Assumptions: τ and σ are stopping times for one filtration (F_k), with ∞ + 1 = ∞. Then min(τ, σ), max(τ, σ) and τ + 1 are stopping times (Proposition 9.6).

front: For a stopping time τ, which events about the time itself lie in F_k?
back: {τ > k} and {τ = k} both lie in F_k, for each whole number k ≥ 0 (Lemma 9.7).

front: For the trivial filtration F_k = {empty set, Ω} at every k, what is a stopping time?
back: It takes one constant value c, in {0, 1, …} ∪ {∞}, on every outcome (Problem R2).

front: How many of the 256 paths of the 8-step fair walk have reached +1 by time 8?
back: 186, a probability of 0.7265625 (Lab 1, Part A).

front: Is any time that depends on the whole path a stopping time?
back: No. Definition 9.1 requires {τ ≤ k} to lie in F_k for each k, so a time that uses step k+1 at time k is excluded (Part B of Lab 1 shows the failure).

front: Is the first hitting time of +1 a stopping time whatever the filtration?
back: No. With the trivial filtration, {τ ≤ 1} = {X_1 = 1} is not in {empty set, Ω}. Proposition 9.5 needs adaptedness, which the natural filtration supplies.

front: Does finiteness on each path make a stopping time bounded?
back: No. For the first time the walk equals +1, the paths with m steps of −1 followed by m + 1 steps of +1 give τ = 2m + 1, and these values have no upper bound as m grows.

front: What are the stopped process M_(τ∧k) and the value M_τ?
back: M_(τ∧k), with τ∧k = min(τ, k), follows M until τ and is then frozen at M_τ. The value M_τ(ω) = M_(τ(ω))(ω) where τ(ω) < ∞ (Definition 10.1).

front: What are the increments of the stopped martingale?
back: Assumptions: M is a martingale on (F_k), τ is a stopping time for the same filtration, and Assumption CE holds (stated, not proved). For each k, M_(τ∧k) is integrable and E[M_(τ∧(k+1))] = E[M_(τ∧k)]. The proof uses M_(τ∧(k+1)) − M_(τ∧k) = 1{τ > k}(M_(k+1) − M_k) (Lemma 10.2).

front: What is optional stopping for a bounded stopping time?
back: Assumptions: (Ω, F, P) is a probability space; M is a martingale on (F_k); τ is a stopping time with a fixed whole number N ≥ 0 and τ(ω) ≤ N for every outcome ω. Assumption CE holds (stated, not proved). Then M_τ is integrable and E[M_τ] = E[M_0] (Theorem 10.3).

front: What is the doubling strategy with capital K?
back: With K ≥ 1 an integer number of cents, bet k is a fair ±1 coin and stakes 2^(k−1) cents. The strategy places bet k only if no earlier bet has won and the stake does not exceed the wealth on hand. Ruin means stopping without a win (Definition 10.5).

front: How many bets does the doubling strategy place with capital K?
back: Let m satisfy 2^m ≤ K + 1 < 2^(m+1). The number of bets is min(w, m), where w is the index of the first win. D is a martingale (under Assumption CE), τ is a stopping time, and τ ≤ m (Lemma 10.6).

front: With capital K, what are the ruin probability and the final wealth?
back: Assumptions: K ≥ 1 is an integer and m is as in Lemma 10.6. Ruin, meaning no win by bet m, has probability 2^(−m). The wealth is K + 1 after a win and K + 1 − 2^m after ruin, and the expected final wealth is K (Proposition 10.7).

front: How many bets, and what win and ruin probabilities, does Lab 1 print for capital K = 1000 cents?
back: 9 bets, a win probability of 0.9980468750, and a ruin probability of 0.0019531250.

front: Without a capital limit, what are P(τ = ∞) and D_τ?
back: Assumptions: the unbounded doubling strategy, with τ the index of the first win and D the net gain. P(τ = ∞) = 0, so τ < ∞ with probability one, and D_τ = 1 almost surely (Proposition 10.9(a)).

front: Does doubling win one cent almost surely, so that the strategy makes money?
back: No. With capital K the strategy wins with probability 1 − 2^(−m), which is 0.9980468750 at K = 1000. But the ruin branch leaves 489 cents, and the expected final wealth is exactly K (Proposition 10.7).

front: Does optional stopping hold for every stopping time of a martingale?
back: Theorem 10.3 needs a fixed bound N. Proposition 10.9 gives a stopping time τ for the doubling process D, with E[D_τ] = 1 while E[D_0] = 0; D is a martingale under Assumption CE (Lemma 10.6).

front: Does a stopping time that is finite with probability one always satisfy E[M_τ] = E[M_0]?
back: No. In the unbounded doubling strategy (Example 10.8), Proposition 10.9(a) gives P(τ < ∞) = 1 and D_τ = 1 almost surely, yet E[D_τ] = 1, not 0 = E[D_0]. Finiteness with probability one is not enough.

front: What is the wealth after ruin in the doubling strategy?
back: With integer K ≥ 1, the wealth after ruin is K + 1 − 2^m cents, where m is as in Lemma 10.6 (Proposition 10.7). This is 0 exactly when K + 1 is a power of two (K = 1, 3, 7, 15, …), and it is not zero in general, so a low ruin probability with small leftover wealth can still give expected final wealth K.

front: What is a nonnegative submartingale?
back: Assumptions: X is adapted to (F_k), with X_k ≥ 0 and E[X_k] < ∞, and E[X_(k+1) 1_A] ≥ E[X_k 1_A] for each k ≥ 0 and each event A in F_k (Definition 11.1). On a finite space this is the same as E[X_(k+1) | F_k] ≥ X_k; on a general space that equivalence uses Assumption CE (L07).

front: Is |S_k| a nonnegative submartingale for the fair walk?
back: Assumptions: X_1, X_2, … are independent steps, each +1 or −1 with probability 1/2; S_0 = 0; the filtration is the natural one. Then |S_k| is a nonnegative submartingale, because (|s + 1| + |s − 1|)/2 = max(1, |s|) ≥ |s| (Lemma 11.2).

front: What is Doob's maximal inequality in its finite-horizon form?
back: Assumptions: (Ω, F, P) is a probability space and (F_k) a filtration; X is a nonnegative submartingale; N ≥ 0 is a fixed whole number and λ > 0. With A = {max_(0≤k≤N) X_k ≥ λ}: λ P(A) ≤ E[X_N 1_A] ≤ E[X_N], so P(max_(0≤k≤N) X_k ≥ λ) ≤ E[X_N]/λ (Theorem 11.3).

front: For the fair walk, what is E[S_N²]?
back: E[S_N²] = N, from the independence and zero mean of the steps (Problem R3).

front: Does Doob's inequality bound the expected maximum?
back: No. For a nonnegative submartingale X, it bounds the probability P(max X_k ≥ λ) by E[X_N]/λ (Corollary 11.4). It does not bound E[max X_k].

front: Does the bound hold for any process with finite expectation, signed or not?
back: No. Nonnegativity is needed. For the signed walk with N = 1 and λ = 1, P(max S_k ≥ 1) = 1/2, while E[S_1]/1 = 0. Part C of Lab 1 prints both values, and the bound fails.

front: Is Doob's bound always loose, since a maximum is rarely as large as the horizon value?
back: No. For |S| of the fair walk with N = 1 and λ = 1, the probability is 1 and the bound is E|S_1|/1 = 1, so the bound is attained. Part A of Lab 1 prints a largest ratio of 1.000000 at N = 1, 2 and 4.

front: For a square-integrable martingale under Assumption OA, what is E[M_m(M_n − M_m)]?
back: Assumptions: (Ω, F, P) is a probability space with a filtration (F_n); M is a square-integrable martingale; 0 ≤ m ≤ n are whole numbers; and Assumption OA holds. Then E[M_m(M_n − M_m)] = 0 (Lemma 12.1). It is Assumption OA applied with Y = M_m.

front: Is the square of the increments from a fixed time a submartingale?
back: Assumptions: M is a square-integrable martingale on (F_n), m ≥ 0 is fixed, and Assumption OA holds (stated, not proved). Then Y_k = (M_k − M_m)² for k ≥ m is a nonnegative submartingale in the sense of Definition 11.1 of L11 (Lemma 12.3).

front: When does a square-integrable martingale converge?
back: Assumptions: (Ω, F, P) is a probability space; (F_n) is a filtration; M is a martingale with each M_n square-integrable; and some real L has E[M_n²] ≤ L for every n. Assumption OA holds (stated, not proved). Then there is an event Ω_0 with probability one on which M_n(ω) converges to a finite limit (Theorem 12.4).

front: What is the general martingale convergence statement?
back: A martingale with sup_n E|M_n| < ∞ converges almost surely to a finite limit. It is stated, not proved, and not graded on the page (Result 12.6).

front: What is the mean-square error of the dyadic martingale for Y(x) = x at level n?
back: Assumptions: [0, 1] carries the length measure, Y(x) = x, and M_n = E[Y | F_n] on the dyadic cells (Example 12.7). For each n ≥ 0, E[(M_n − Y)²] = 1/(12·4^n) (Proposition 12.8(a)).

front: What is the dyadic martingale for Y(x) = x?
back: M_n = E[Y | F_n], where F_n is generated by the level-n dyadic cells on [0, 1] under the length measure. On a cell, M_n equals the cell's midpoint, so M_n(x) is the midpoint of the cell that contains x (Example 12.7).

front: What are the limit and the expectations of the all-heads martingale?
back: Assumptions: H_1, H_2, … are independent fair flips; F_n = σ(H_1, …, H_n); M_n = 2^n if the first n flips are heads, and 0 otherwise (Example 12.9). Then M_n → 0 almost surely, E[lim M_n] = 0, and E|M_n − lim M_n| = 1 for each n (Proposition 12.10).

front: What is the largest grid error that Lab 1 prints for the dyadic martingale at level 10?
Does a martingale that converges almost surely have the same expectation in the limit as at the start?
back: No. In Example 12.9 (independent fair flips), E[M_0] = 1, while M_n → 0 almost surely, so E[lim M_n] = 0 (Proposition 12.10).

front: If the mean-square error of the dyadic martingale tends to zero, does every path converge to Y?
back: Not from the mean-square error alone, since it averages over x. The pointwise bound |M_n(x) − x| ≤ 2^(−(n+1)) of Proposition 12.8(c) gives convergence at each x.

front: Does the martingale convergence theorem say that the sequence converges to its expectation?
back: No. The limit is a random variable. In Example 12.7 the limit is Y(x) = x, which is not the constant E[Y] = 1/2.

front: What is a σ-finite measure space?
back: A measure space (Ω, F, μ) for which Ω is a countable union of sets of finite measure (Section 2). Each space in the lesson is finite or the unit square with area, and each is σ-finite.

front: What is the product σ-algebra F1 ⊗ F2?
back: The smallest σ-algebra on Ω1 × Ω2 that contains every rectangle A × B with A in F1 and B in F2 (Section 2).

front: When is a process adapted to a filtration?
back: When each X_k is F_k-measurable, so X_k is constant on each cell of the partition at time k and its value is known at time k (Definition 1.1).

front: What does it mean for a martingale to be square-integrable?
back: Each M_n has E[M_n²] < ∞ for every n (Section 1).

front: What is Assumption OA (orthogonality of increments on a general space)?
back: For a square-integrable martingale M on a filtration (F_n) of a probability space, 0 ≤ m ≤ n and every F_m-measurable Y with E[Y²] < ∞, E[Y(M_n − M_m)] = 0. It is stated, not proved, and carries no grade (Section 1).

front: How many of the 729 ordered disjoint pairs fail additivity for ν(A) = (|A|/6)² on the six-point set?
back: 602 pairs. Additivity fails exactly when both sets of the pair are non-empty (Lab 2).
basis: Lab 2, basis: exhaustive enumeration of the six-point space

back: Part B: I_1 = (1/2)(1 − sqrt(1/2)) ≈ 0.1464, a floating-point value.

back: n = 6 at x = 1/5 and n = 51 at x = 1/50. In both cases this is floor(1/x) + 1.

basis: Lab 4, basis: exact fraction computation over the listed values

front: Does the biased walk with p = 1/3 pass the cell test on the ten-step tree?
back: No. It passes none of the 1023 cells at levels 0 to 9, and its first-cell increment is −1/3 at every level, which is 2p − 1 (Lab 1 Part B; Proposition 2.3).

front: Does the look-ahead rule of Lab 1 Part B pass the stopping-time test?
back: No. It fails at each k from 0 to 7. At k = 8 its event depends on all 8 steps, so the test can pass there.

What does countable subadditivity say for a measure μ?
back: Assumptions: (Ω, F) is a σ-algebra with a measure μ, and A_1, A_2, … are events. Then μ(∪_n A_n) ≤ Σ_n μ(A_n) (Proposition 1.3(c)).

front: What does continuity from below say for a measure μ?
back: Assumptions: (Ω, F) is a σ-algebra with a measure μ, and A_1 ⊆ A_2 ⊆ … are events with union A. Then μ(A_n) → μ(A) as n → ∞ (Proposition 1.3(d)).

front: On a finite set, if a density of ν with respect to μ exists, what does it force?
back: Assumptions: Ω is finite, and μ and ν are measures given by non-negative weights. If ν has a density with respect to μ, then ν ≪ μ (Theorem 2.2(c)).

front: Without a capital limit, what are E[D_τ] and D_0?
back: Assumptions: the unbounded doubling strategy, with τ and D as in Example 10.8. E[D_τ] = 1, while D_0 = 0 (Proposition 10.9(b)).

front: In the unbounded doubling strategy under Assumption CE, what is E[D_{τ∧n}] for each whole number n ≥ 0?
back: Assumptions: the unbounded doubling strategy of Example 10.8, and Assumption CE holds (stated, not proved). Then E[D_{τ∧n}] = 0 for every whole number n ≥ 0 (Proposition 10.9(c)).

front: What is E[M_n²] for the dyadic martingale for Y(x) = x at level n?
back: Assumptions: [0, 1] carries the length measure, Y(x) = x, and M_n = E[Y | F_n] on the dyadic cells (Example 12.7). For each n ≥ 0, E[M_n²] = 1/3 − 1/(12·4^n) (Proposition 12.8(b)).

front: What pointwise bound does the dyadic martingale for Y(x) = x satisfy at level n?
back: Assumptions: [0, 1] carries the length measure, Y(x) = x, and M_n = E[Y | F_n] on the dyadic cells (Example 12.7). For each n ≥ 0, |M_n(x) − x| ≤ 2^(−(n+1)) for every x in [0, 1], so M_n(x) → x for every x (Proposition 12.8(c)).

front: For a square-integrable martingale under Assumption OA, what is E[(M_n − M_m)²]?
back: Assumptions: (Ω, F, P) is a probability space with a filtration (F_n); M is a square-integrable martingale; 0 ≤ m ≤ n are whole numbers; and Assumption OA holds. Then E[(M_n − M_m)²] = E[M_n²] − E[M_m²] (Lemma 12.1).

front: For a square-integrable martingale under Assumption OA, how do E[M_m²] and E[M_n²] compare for m ≤ n?
back: Assumptions: (Ω, F, P) is a probability space with a filtration (F_n); M is a square-integrable martingale; 0 ≤ m ≤ n are whole numbers; and Assumption OA holds. Then E[M_m²] ≤ E[M_n²] (Lemma 12.1).

front: Which candidate family on the four-point set fails Lab 1's closure checks, and why?
back: The candidate {empty set, {0,1}, whole set} fails complement closure, because its complement {2,3} is missing.
basis: Lab 1, basis: exhaustive enumeration of finite families

front: For the fair walk, what bound does Doob's inequality give on P(max over k ≤ N of |S_k| ≥ c)?
back: P(max over k ≤ N of |S_k| ≥ c) ≤ N/c² for c > 0. Problem R3 derives it from Corollary 11.4 with Z_k = S_k² and E[S_N²] = N.
